newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's sluggish economy to top ministerial agenda.
newsitem.headline: EU's sluggish economy to top ministerial agenda.

text.p: European Union finance ministers are expected to conclude on Monday that the EU's economic recovery is largely on track, but that the pace of growth is not fast enough to generate sufficient jobs growth.
The ECOFIN Council will focus its attention on the European Commission's annual economic report, which urges governments to adopt greater labour market flexibility to fight double-digit unemployment.
In its lengthy review, the EU's executive forecast on Thursday that a faster pace of economic growth would have only a limited impact on the current 10.8 percent EU jobless rate.
"The moderate strengthening of employment growth in the Community in the coming years is expected to be sufficient to achieve only a modest reduction in unemployment," the report said.
Europe's jobless problem has come into sharper focus as Germany, the EU's main economic engine, struggles under the weight of nearly 4.7 million unemployed, the highest level since the 1930s.
The record unemployment rate has raised doubts over Bonn's ability to reign in expenditure and bring its deficit in line with the Maastricht treaty's target.
Under growing political pressure, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel has not yet announced how he plans to deal with an expected shortfall in revenue.
The opposition Social Democrats have called for a supplementary budget, while a senior Free Democratic Party official called earlier this week for a freeze on government spending.
Independent economists have reckoned that the high unemployment rate would add between 10 and 18 billion marks to German government spending.
Separately, the finance ministers are expected to endorse the efforts Belgium has made towards meeting the Maastricht treaty's criteria on deficits, interest rates and inflation.
"Everyone is convinced the Belgian programme is a good one," said one EU diplomat.
In March, the ministers will review new economic convergence plans from Germany and France, diplomats added.
Waigel is also expected to brief his colleagues on last weekend's Berlin meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised nations.
